content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated, nonfat cappuccino is a beverage made from roasted coffee beans that have had the caffeine removed and skimmed milk. It retains the characteristic coffee aroma and creamy texture while providing minimal calories and virtually no fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Caffeine is removed by a water‑based extraction process that preserves most flavor compounds.
Nonfat milk creates a lighter drink but still allows a stable foam thanks to added emulsifiers.
Traditional cappuccino is served in a 150–180 ml cup with equal parts espresso, steamed milk, and milk foam.
Decaf coffees often use Arabica beans because their milder flavor survives the decaffeination process better.
In some countries, decaf cappuccino is finished with a sprinkle of cinnamon or cocoa powder for extra aroma.

items.title: Low Calorie Content
items.content: Skimmed milk and the absence of caffeine make this drink suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee retains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive Comfort
items.content: Without caffeine, the beverage is gentler on the stomach for people with sensitivity.

items.title: Reduced Cardiovascular Risk
items.content: Studies associate moderate coffee consumption, including decaf, with a lower risk of heart disease.

items.title: Mood Enhancement
items.content: The aromatic profile of coffee stimulates serotonin production even without caffeine.

items.title: Acid Sensitivity
items.content: Coffee remains acidic and may cause discomfort for those with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Milk Allergy
items.content: Skimmed milk can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Residues from Decaffeination
items.content: Some decaffeination methods use solvents; choose products labeled “natural decaffeination” to minimize exposure.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve the decaf cappuccino hot, immediately after preparation to preserve the foam. A pinch of cinnamon, nutmeg, or a small amount of sweetener can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ground decaf coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Skimmed milk should be used within 5–7 days after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: Dark green vegetables such as spinach, broccoli, kale and collard greens are often used as an ingredient in omelets. They give the dish a vivid color, rich flavor and boost its nutritional value thanks to high levels of vitamins, minerals and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark‑green leafy vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, which has antioxidant properties.
Spinach contains more iron than beef, and its plant‑based iron is better absorbed when paired with vitamin C.
Broccoli provides sulforaphane, a compound studied for its potential anti‑cancer effects.
Kale is considered one of the most nutrient‑dense vegetables, offering over 200 % of the daily value of vitamin K per 100 g.
These vegetables can be used as natural food coloring in culinary applications.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Includes folate (B9), essential for DNA synthesis and anemia prevention.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Enhances iron absorption from plant foods and supports immune function.

items.title: Excellent source of vitamin K
items.content: Important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Calcium, magnesium and potassium support heart, muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar and promotes satiety.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Some dark greens (e.g., spinach) contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables like broccoli can cause gas when eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rare, but possible allergies to specific leafy greens may occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add dark green vegetables to an omelet either raw or lightly sautéed first. Chop them finely so they distribute evenly in the egg mixture. Pair with a modest amount of cheese and herbs to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, stored in a perforated bag. Use within 3–5 days. For freezing, blanch briefly before packing to preserve color and nutrients.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a beef patty, bun, lettuce leaf, tomato slice, onion, cheese and sauce. The NFS (New Flavor Series) version features an upgraded beef patty recipe, a softer bun, and a signature sauce with smoked pepper notes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair.
The word “hamburger” comes from the German city of Hamburg, where similar meat patties were popular in the 19th century.
The NFS variant was co‑developed with a renowned chef who added smoked pepper to the sauce.
The world’s largest hamburger weighed over 1 ton and was made in the USA in 2012.
In Japan, “rice burgers” replace the bun with pressed rice cakes.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc helps maintain a healthy immune system and aids wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excess saturated fat intake can raise blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: Sauces and condiments often contain high sodium, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric content
items.content: One NFS hamburger can contain 500–800 kcal, so it should be accounted for in daily energy balance.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bun typically contains wheat; people with celiac disease should choose a gluten‑free option.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hamburger hot, split the bun, and place the patty with toppings inside. It’s convenient to eat with hands, but a fork and knife can be used if the bun is very soft. For a lighter taste, add fresh vegetables or swap the sauce for a yogurt‑based dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared hamburgers are best eaten immediately. If you need to store them, cool them in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Reheat using an oven or grill to keep the bun from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup with wonton is a traditional Chinese dish consisting of a flavorful broth with delicate wonton dumplings, usually filled with meat, seafood, or vegetables. The dish offers a light yet rich taste and is often garnished with green onions, ginger, and soy sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wonton comes from the Chinese word “馄饨”, meaning “soft pouch”.
Wonton soup is commonly served on festive occasions, especially in northern China.
Traditionally, wontons are hand‑folded, shaping the dough into a half‑moon and sealing the edges with fingers.
Regional variations exist: Shanghai favors shrimp, while Beijing prefers pork with green onion.
The broth can be based on chicken, pork, or seafood, influencing aroma and color.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Wonton fillings often contain meat or seafood, providing a complete source of high‑quality protein.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The clear broth is typically low in fat, making the dish suitable for light meals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables added to the soup (e.g., carrots, spinach) contribute vitamin A, C, and potassium.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: Collagen boost
items.content: Bone‑based broths contain gelatin and collagen, beneficial for joints and digestion.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce commonly used in the broth raises salt levels; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: If the filling includes shrimp or fish, allergic individuals may react.

items.title: Preparation difficulty
items.content: The thin wonton wrapper can tear easily, requiring skill and care.

items.title: Storage contamination
items.content: Fresh dough and fillings spoil quickly at room temperature; keep them refrigerated and cook promptly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot in a deep bowl. Eat wontons with chopsticks or a fork, and sip the broth with a spoon. Common garnishes include sliced green onion, cilantro, chili, or a splash of vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Wontons can be frozen on a tray, then transferred to a bag for up to 2 months; thaw and bring to a boil before serving.
